title: Food Chain and Food Web

mcqs.question: Which ecological pyramid is ALWAYS upright?
Approximately what percentage of energy transfers between trophic levels?
An inverted pyramid of numbers occurs when:
options: One large producer supports many small consumers

notes: Food chain: a linear sequence of organisms where each is eaten by the next; transfers energy and matter (sun → producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer).
Food web: a network of interconnected food chains; more realistic than a single chain; shows multiple feeding relationships.
Trophic levels: TL1 producers (autotrophs), TL2 primary consumers (herbivores), TL3 secondary consumers (carnivores), TL4+ tertiary consumers.
Ecological pyramids: number (pyramid of numbers), biomass (pyramid of biomass), energy (pyramid of energy).
Pyramid of energy: always upright; each level has less energy than the one below (10% rule).
Pyramid of numbers: usually upright; can be inverted (e.g., one tree supports many insects).
Pyramid of biomass: usually upright; can be inverted in aquatic ecosystems (phytoplankton turn over fast).
Productivity: gross primary productivity (GPP = total photosynthesis), net primary productivity (NPP = GPP − plant respiration).
Consumer productivity: energy assimilated by consumers per unit time.
NEB focus: food chain, food web, trophic levels, ecological pyramids, and productivity.
confusion: A food chain is LINEAR; a food web is a NETWORK of chains (more realistic).
Producers (plants, phytoplankton) are at trophic level 1; herbivores at level 2; carnivores at level 3+.
The pyramid of ENERGY is always upright; the pyramids of numbers and biomass CAN be inverted.
An inverted pyramid of numbers occurs when one large organism supports many small ones (e.g., a tree with many insects).
An inverted pyramid of biomass occurs in aquatic ecosystems where phytoplankton (producers) have low standing biomass but high turnover.
The 10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers from one trophic level to the next; ~90% is lost as heat.
practice: Draw a food chain for a grassland ecosystem (4 trophic levels).
Draw a food web for a pond ecosystem.
Explain the three types of ecological pyramids.
Calculate NPP from GPP and plant respiration.
Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright.
universalFacts: The 10% rule (Lindeman, 1942) explains why food chains are usually 4–5 trophic levels long.
A pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright because energy is lost at each transfer (heat, respiration).
Phytoplankton in the ocean produce ~50% of Earth's oxygen (GPP of aquatic ecosystems).
NPP is the energy available to consumers (herbivores) in an ecosystem.
examples: Grassland food chain: grass → rabbit → fox → eagle (4 trophic levels).
Pond food web: algae → mosquito larva → frog → snake → eagle; also algae → zooplankton → small fish → big fish.
Inverted pyramid of numbers: one oak tree (TL1) → many aphids (TL2) → a few ladybirds (TL3).
Inverted pyramid of biomass: phytoplankton (TL1) → zooplankton (TL2) → small fish (TL3) in the ocean.
Productivity: GPP = 1000 gC/m²/yr; plant respiration = 500 gC/m²/yr → NPP = 500 gC/m²/yr.

Explain the three types of ecological pyramids.
Define trophic levels and give one example of each.
Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright.
Calculate NPP from GPP and respiration (given values).
formulas: Food chain: Producer (TL1) → Primary consumer (TL2) → Secondary consumer (TL3) → Tertiary consumer (TL4)
10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers between trophic levels
GPP = total photosynthesis; NPP = GPP − plant respiration (R)
Pyramid of energy: always upright; each level < the one below
keyPoints: Food chain = linear; food web = network of chains.
Trophic levels: TL1 producers, TL2 herbivores, TL3 carnivores, TL4+ top carnivores.
Three pyramids: number, biomass, energy.
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright; number and biomass can be inverted.
10% rule: ~10% energy transfers between levels.
Productivity: GPP (total), NPP (GPP − respiration).
NPP is the energy available to herbivores.
enrichedContent.summary: Energy and matter flow through ecosystems in food chains (linear) and food webs (networks). Trophic levels (producers → primary consumers → secondary → tertiary) structure these. Ecological pyramids (number, biomass, energy) visualise trophic structure; the pyramid of energy is always upright because ~90% of energy is lost at each transfer (10% rule). Productivity (GPP, NPP) measures the rate of energy capture and availability to consumers. NEB focuses on food chains, food webs, trophic levels, the three pyramids, and productivity calculations.
